title: Joyfully Impossible - The Bodhisattva Vows
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett invites listeners to contemplate the Bodhisattva vows as a means of cultivating wisdom, compassion, and interconnectedness, rather than solely focusing on individual salvation. They propose a revised interpretation that emphasizes mutual support and facilitation, encouraging participants to approach their personal vows with patience, self-generosity, and a willingness to listen deeply to others. By doing so, Nomon hopes to foster a sense of community and shared understanding among those who participate in this practice.

But we'll try to do it in such a way that it's still interesting to just show up whenever you can show up, and maybe even more interesting if you're able, for a stretch of time, for a month or something, to say, "I'm going to get down there every Wednesday and hear the next talk on the Heart Sutra or the such-and-so teaching."

His other stuff makes it sound like you're supposed to understand or something.

I'm open to that.

It says in the Lotus Sutra that that's the Dharma we revere and are excited about.

What's cool about Chinese is that there are so many different characters, and when you put a block of four or six or eight of them together in a certain order, there's not that many times, even in thousands of pages, that that exact block of characters reappears.

So they could find that same block of characters that's behind our English translation there in the Lotus Sutra, and they can be pretty confident that whoever created that chant was quoting the Lotus Sutra.
That's pretty fun.
It's fun to have a little sense of where things come from.

Dogen loved the Lotus Sutra.
He quotes it all the time.

Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.

So if you've been before, that should all sound familiar.

I don't really remember what I said or thought or felt at the moment, but it really brought me up short, these four lines.
I didn't pause to try to figure it out or read the surrounding text, because there were blocks of text all around it, which must have had some context for why they were quoting it.

I just took a breath and was impressed.
Like, wow.

Well, maybe the first thing you notice about these four vows, if you think about them, and it's totally legit to just chant this stuff and not think about it too much, that's fine, we maybe overthink things as it is, but if you think about it, one thing you probably notice right away is how utterly impossible these vows are.
I don't know that I could save one being.
I don't know if I could save myself.
What does it even mean to save anything or anybody?
Not to mention numberless beings.
The second one, and if you want to look at these in your chant book, if that helps you stay oriented, it's on the page we just had open: the one about delusions.
Well, that seems a little more approachable, don't you think?
Maybe you have a handle on a few of your delusions and can notice them and release from them.

A little later, I thought, oh yeah, that was me being, I was pent-up aggression, or that was impatience, or that was assuming something, and so on and so forth.
That was whatever it was.

So sometimes you notice your delusions after the fact, but it must be that the vast amount of our delusions we're unaware of, and we take for reality and feel justified in, and it's just part of how it is, right, being ourselves.
So this vow that they're inexhaustible, yeah, that seems true, right?
That we'll end them all, that we'll be free from them, that we won't be caught by any of them: that's impossible.
And the next one, about Dharma gates, to enter all the Dharma gates, I've always felt a little encouraged by that one.
How about you?
It's also impossible, but it seems like less of a bummer that I'll never accomplish that, because it'd be fun to try, right?
And a Dharma gate could be anything.
It's not just reading a verse in a book or going to a Dharma talk or sitting in formal meditation, right?
Maybe it's working with those delusions.
Maybe that's a Dharma gate.
It's some way that we're opening to the way it is, some way we're using wisdom and compassion, using teachings.

Maybe it's navigating something difficult with a friend, or maybe it's in some way responding to our current insane political situation with a little more something, a little more wisdom or a little more compassion, maybe.
There are a lot of Dharma gates we're aware of, and sometimes we do veer away from them, for sure.
We're tentative or we're tired or we're scared.
We can notice ourselves passing up Dharma gates, but then we can notice ourselves entering Dharma gates.
But just like the other two before it, there must be boundless other Dharma gates we're completely unaware of, entering them or not entering them.
We don't perceive them.
And yeah, then we have becoming Buddha.
We often do say here that it's not about becoming Buddha, although the vow sounds that way, but more like dropping the delusion that we aren't Buddha.
And that's a delusion, so that's back to the second one.
This is the usual way of these little sets of teachings: one of them always refers to all the other ones, and they are all interdependent and interpenetrated.
So one thing that's nice is you don't have to remember all the stuff.
Just pay attention to the one in whatever the list of things is that really speaks to you, because it's going to contain all the others.
That can be your one.
Just work with that.
Not be constantly like, what are the other ones?
The eight of this, ten of that: list and list and list and list.
So I dug into this a little bit, just curious where they came from.
And bizarrely, there's also an origin story here in the Lotus Sutra.
Maybe it all just comes back to the Lotus Sutra in the end.
Why do we study anything else?
We know this because of the Tiantai master, Tiantai being another form of Buddhism in China, in the sixth century, the 500s, named Master Ji Yi, romanized Z-H-I-Y-I.
It's hard to make it out when you hear it: Ji Yi.
He came up with proto-bodhisattva vows.
It is clear the Zen people took his idea and worked with it.
So I'll share a little bit about that.
This is what I was going to put on the screen, so maybe next time I'll show you.
His first version was a quotation from the Lotus Sutra, which he then commented on, and then later, in a later work, he did another version that's pretty close to our Bodhisattva vows.
So here's the one that's quoting directly from the Lotus Sutra.
If you've studied the Lotus Sutra, this is in the Medicine Plants chapter.
*Those not yet ferried across, I will cause to cross.
Those not yet understanding, I will cause to understand.
Those not yet at peace, I will cause to be at peace.
Those not yet in nirvana, I will cause to obtain nirvana.*
One thing to notice in there is that little verb phrase that repeats, "I will cause."
It uses an underlying Chinese word that means exactly that: I'm going to make it happen.
I'm your guy.
I'm going to help you.
I'm going to make you understand and be at peace and obtain nirvana, which is deep, deep ultimate peace.
And "ferried across" is a reference.
It's all in Buddhism, all over the place, that we're on the side of the river where things are nuts.
That's true.
The world of conditions and greed, hate, and delusion, and then also love and passion and everything else.
And there's a river to cross to get to the other side, and the other side is nirvana.
Maybe it's a pretty wide river, maybe with a really fast current, hard to cross.
So "ferried across" is directly referring to that.
So this is the initial version, just coming straight from the Lotus Sutra.
I haven't actually found it in the Lotus Sutra myself, but I shall.
Then in later work, here's one that's like a proto version of the Bodhisattva vows.
It'll be easier when you see this.
*Those not yet saved from suffering, I'll cause them to be saved.
Those not yet understanding the cause, I will cause them to understand.*
So suffering, that's the same as saving beings.
And this is more for noble truths now.
Delusions are definitely involved in the cause of suffering, so it all connects.
The third one in this proto vows:
*Those not yet at peace in the path, I cause them to be at peace.*
So that's entering Dharma gates, the path, also the third noble truth.
*Those not yet attaining cessation, I will cause them to attain it.*
It sounds in English pretty far from our Bodhisattva vows, but there's more overlap with the Chinese characters than you quite hear in the English.
But then what are definitely recognizably our Bodhisattva vows show up for the first time, at least amongst the texts that survive, like who knows what really happened thousands of years ago.
This is in the Platform Sutra, which is a famous, famous sutra telling the most important early stories of Buddhism in China, famous stories that shaped the tradition from then on.
It turns out historically, maybe none of it actually happened, but it's all the more important to the way it's thought about.
And with this sutra, the Platform Sutra, there are two main versions that are hundreds of years apart.
So this literature is not just like the Buddha said it 3,000 years ago and it stayed intact, right?
It's like any other human thing, even if it's humans inspired by Buddha or humans who are Buddha.
Things change over time.
So there's an earlier version which was found in this huge cache of documents.
This was like the most important discovery in Buddhist studies ever.
Right around 1900, I think it was 1911 or something like that, they discovered this massive cave in the desert east of China, in a little oasis town called Donghuang.
A huge library had been sealed up, with thousands and thousands of scrolls of Buddhist texts.
Buddhist scholars have been reading it ever since.
I don't know that they've processed it all to this day.
Anyway, there's a version of the Platform Sutra in that stash which was dated to the 8th century.

So this is a couple of hundred years later, when the other master, who was in a previous school, or a cousin school, I guess you could say, like the Tiantai school, are like our older cousins and we were the upstarts.
Probably the Tiantai people are like, "Oh man, they're kind of bratty, jeez.
I think they know everything."
So in there, that sutra has Huineng, the central character, sharing this vow:
*I vow to save the limitless beings of my mind.
I vow to cut the infinite afflictions of my mind.
I vow to learn the boundless Dharma gates of my own mind.
I vow to complete the supreme Buddha way of...*
Oh, sorry, I said that one wrong.
I'm going to start over.
*I vow to save the limitless beings of my own mind.
I vow to cut the infinite afflictions of my own mind.
I vow to learn the boundless Dharma gates of my own nature.*
It changes there.
*I vow to learn the boundless Dharma gates of my own nature.
I vow to complete the supreme Buddha way of my own nature.*
So you can basically hear our vows in there.
But Zen, through this sutra and through the character of Huineng, brings it home in a certain way, right?
The earlier version was: I see all you suffering beings out there, I'm going to fix it.
It had that strong verb that meant I'm going to cause this to happen.
This version loses that verb, which is Chan in Chinese, and replaces it with vow.
Instead of saying, "I'm going to do it," I vow to do it.
So there's a totally different flavor to that, right?
It's aspiration.
It's still serious, like I'm doing something, I'm committed.
But I'm not saying that I'm the one doing it.
I'm vowing to do it.
I'm vowing that it somehow happens.
And it's not you beings out there.
I recognize that it's all happening through my mind and through my nature, which is the nature of everything.
So the first two, he says, of my own mind.
So there's some degree of transformational work around the mind that's afflicted and suffering, right?
But the second two, with Dharma and Buddha, have something to do with the nature of the universe, being more in harmony with the nature of the universe.
So it's also not causing it to happen, right?
It's being more in accord with.
So that's like the proto-proto version, right before our version.
And then exactly the same characters that we chant are found in a later version of the same sutra, the Platform Sutra.
This is dated from the 13th century.
So what's that, 500 years later?
That version became the standard thing that most everybody would chant, and it's the main one translated.
If you've read up on this stuff, Red Pine goes back to the old one, one of his choices.
But more often, it's this later one that's studied.
It's kind of like tidied.
They added some stuff and smoothed some rough edges and maybe added the learning of 500 years of practice.
So it's not necessarily a worse one because it's tidied up and a little less raw.
In that version, they also wanted something that chanted well.
We can't really hear the chanting in Chinese here because I couldn't pronounce it properly.

But they made the lines all the same number of characters, so it's a block of four lines of seven characters each that says what we chant: that sentient beings are limitless, boundless, I vow to save them.
And here's a pretty literal translation, actually.
Ours has a little bit of gloss in it to make it nicer in English.
But here's a very literal translation from the seven characters per line in Chinese:
*Beings limitless, vow to save.
Afflictions limitless, vow to sever.
Dharma gates limitless, vow to learn or study.
Unsurpassed Buddha way, vow to complete.*
So you can hear it's right there.
This actually sounds good in Chinese and sounds pretty good in Sino-Japanese and sounds perfectly decent in English.
So you can see a kind of evolution here in all kinds of ways: a sense of more integration and less of a sense of separateness, which is Zen's hallmark, right?
Not to buy into so much this idea of separateness, of this and that, which they fancily called dualistic thinking.
To free yourself from dualistic thinking.
And that sort of radical inner penetration that Dogen was talking about all the time, that if one being is saved, all beings are saved, and this is that being, right?
This is that being.
But speaking of saving, the character that the translators translate as "to save" is a pretty interesting one.
I'm looking forward to showing you this on the screen another week.
It actually has an original Chinese meaning, which is just to measure.
How did "to measure" end up being "to save"?
Well, it turns out that the Chinese translators in the fourth, fifth, sixth centuries mainly had some big problems to solve when they were trying to figure out how to translate Sanskrit Buddhism.

Sanskrit Buddhism is loaded with complex terminology, in ways that everyday Sanskrit words got reused and new Sanskrit words were invented, and that had already been happening for six, eight hundred years, right?
So they had to figure out how to make all this work in Chinese with its set of characters and sounds.

One of the ones that really flummoxed them, apparently, I was reading a scholarly book about this, at least bits of it, was a word we were talking about on Sunday, the word paramita, which means something like "to go beyond" or can also be translated as "perfect."
It's put with important qualities for us to practice, like generosity paramita, generosity that goes beyond generosity.
At first, one of the things they would do was just to try to transliterate a Sanskrit word.
But that must have been really hard for the Chinese to read, because what they were doing was picking kind of random characters that made the right sounds.
If you look at the characters in terms of meaning, it would have looked like gibberish.
I'll try to think of an English version that makes some kind of sense.
Seven banana mountain rice or something, and you're like, what?
But then you have to listen in your mind to the sounds, and the sounds are like these Sanskrit sounds, which you've never necessarily even heard before, right?
So at first they used four characters to transliterate paramita.
But then some genius decided that this character, just pronounced du, would be a much better thing to do.
Just one character that everyone would learn, this is what it's being used for.
And it's this character, to measure.
Later scholars believe the logic was something like, well, if I can measure the river, I can find a way across.
I can take the measure of reality and find a way to go beyond it.
Because it doesn't mean save, it means going beyond.
It means crossing and going beyond.
And so in our vow, our numberless-beings vow to save them, that's the character that's used.
It's not actually a character that means to save, but it means to help across, which kind of means to save.
So I think in our case, we're probably the result of 19th century English and other European scholars who were all Christians, or at least brought up in the church.
And there's this idea of salvation, right?
To carry someone across is not salvation.
It's to save them, like you pray and, you know, the missionaries were saving people.
So I suspect we have this Christian missionary mishmash in our vows.
Darn.
At least we know what it means.
It's okay.
It's like, okay, save.
We can mean whatever we want by save.
But think about it that way.
Look at that line in the book there:
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to help them across.*
It's a different feeling, right, than saving them.
It's a lot closer to the meaning of the characters.
Or maybe "I help" implies I'm separate from them, and the whole thing from Huineng about in my mind, with my mind, that's not quite it.
So maybe it's something like "sentient beings are boundless, crossing together" or something like that.
How about that?
Crossing together.
I vow to cross together.
We will all cross together.
We will all go beyond together.
Which means you're doing something, right?
You're showing up.
You're not just like, "Yeah, take me with you when you go."
You're doing something.
But you're not fixing anybody or saving anybody.
You're being in some way a facilitator and a support for what we all need.
And thus we all need together, right?
So yeah, this was really fun for me.
And this is all, by the way, inspired by a book from Nelson Foster called *Rediscovering the Treasures of* ling.
He kind of got into this too.
This is one of the characters he got interested in.
I had read that a while ago, and then I was trying to study the vows and thought, oh my gosh, that's the one Nelson talked about.
So let's talk a little bit about what these vows actually mean for us and not just let me geek out for the whole time.
I thought we'd do a practice, which we'll practice tonight, of being in a small group with some structure.
A structured conversation.
Sometimes we call this monologues because one person is going to speak at a time.
Well, "monologue" usually sounds like the person is being boring.
This is anything but boring.
We'll have a topic, usually a kind of broad topic.
Here it can be reading these vows and looking at these vows, whether you're looking at them for the first time tonight or have chanted them a thousand times.
How do they speak to you?
What do they mean to you?
Do one or two of those four seem more important or more valuable or more useful or more annoying or more intimidating or more something?
What do you think about this bit about save not really being saved, in that kind of theological saving way?
The nice thing here is that you have a lot of support to explore out loud.
You don't have to have a clue what you're going to say.
If your mind is constricting, see what happens.
It's a patience practice.
I'll see what happens.
Kind of being generous with yourself.
You'll have five minutes to see what comes out of your mouth.
There could be a fair amount of silence in there too as you read them and breathe and wonder what matters here to you.
If nothing really comes, then you can sit quietly.
If anybody can listen without needing you to say anything, it would be this gang, right?
You'll be in little groups of three, did I say that?
The other two of you will just be deeply listening.
Just present, just listening.
Not interjecting.
Not like, "Yeah, yeah, you got this," or "Me too."
A little nodding and smiling is okay.
We can't help it.
But just be relaxed and kind and warm and listen to the person whose turn it is to speak.
I'll use a bell to time it too, so you won't have to keep track of the time.
Just see what comes up for us around living these vows.
What are they?
What are they for you?
And also recognize that any answer you give is completely provisional, what's coming to you now and subject to revision.
We're not going to be like, next week we'll see you and say, "Did you da-da-da-da?"
No, no, no.
In fact, why don't we just forget about whatever the person said, with love, not with forgetfulness.
We'll just leave it here.
What's said in the Zendo, that kind of thing.
Is that Rome or Vegas usually?
Okay, so once you find yourself a group of two, maybe people you're just meeting or people you know, doesn't matter.
We can rearrange the cushions a little bit, make a little jumble of the Zendo and get tight in with your little triad.
Once everybody's found their people, I'll ring the bell and talk you through it.
And Zoomers, Aiden can put you in a breakout so you can talk.
Oh, hey Debra.
You can talk to me maybe.
There's two of me.
So I'll get them going and then we can both unmute and talk a little bit.
Just a sec.
More or less groups of three, huh?
It's good you're meeting each other and exchanging names, and then all you really need is one volunteer to be the first speaker.
Anybody feeling courageous?
Then let's just sit in silence for a minute to settle the space.
I'll ring the bell.
Close your eyes if you want or lower your gaze, just to relax into this new configuration here.
Feels different, right?
When the bell rings, the first person can start speaking when you're ready, and the other two just deeply listening.
What do these vows mean to you?
Maybe they don't mean anything you want to talk about.
That's fine also.
